speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I am delivering this Ministerial Statement for two purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am a former trade negotiator at the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) when I was a civil servant.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I worked with a very dedicated team, who has over two decades fought hard for the interest of Singapore, to expand the economic and political space for our small island state.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I feel I owe a duty to correct the falsehoods.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Indeed, Singaporean PMEs, like PMEs in other advanced economies, are facing challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If anything, they are part of the solution.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: FTAs and CECA have been made political scapegoats to discredit the policy of the People's Action Party (PAP) Government.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second reason to deliver this Ministerial Statement is to put in context, on behalf of the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and MTI, the Parliamentary Questions that have been posed to the Ministries concerning foreign PMEs, FTAs and CECA.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Tan See Leng will further elaborate on the answers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Taken together, Dr Tan and I will address Oral Question Nos 1 to 3 and Written Question Nos 19 to 24 from yesterday's Order Paper; and Oral Question Nos 1 to 6 and Written Question Nos 40 to 42 from today's Order Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Several of the questions were filed by the Progress Singapore Party's (PSP's) two Non-Constituency Members of Parliament to gather data for a subsequent debate on a Motion they intend to file.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, where we can, we will provide relevant data to equip all parties for that subsequent debate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As I mentioned, for months now, the PSP has alleged that FTAs and CECA have led to the unfettered inflow of Indian professionals, displacing Singaporeans from their jobs and bringing about all kinds of social ills.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a seductively simplistic argument that workers facing challenges at their workplaces can identify with and has stirred up a lot of emotions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: CECA-themed websites have sprouted, filled with quite disturbing xenophobic views about Indian immigrants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Toxic views turned into verbal and physical assaults on Indians, including our citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is sad that serious issues concerning the economic well-being of our country and workers have descended to this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why the Minister for Law called out such xenophobic behaviour during the May Sitting of this House and challenged the PSP to table a Motion on CECA so that the matter could receive a proper public airing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The PSP has since made a public statement on the matter, standing by its view on FTAs and CECA.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It filed various Parliamentary Questions requesting for more data and information.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, I will talk about the following: one, what is fundamental to Singapore's ability to earn a living and survive; two, why FTAs, including CECA, advance our interest and are not the cause of the challenges faced by our workers; and three, what then are the causes of Singaporeans' concerns and how do we address them?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Tan will provide detailed answers to the specific questions, including providing the data which will be useful for our subsequent debate and putting that data in context.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Simply put, we are too small to survive on our own and we need to tap into the global markets to earn a living and be self-reliant.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have no natural resources but we have one precious natural endowment and that is our geographical location.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a lasting advantage but one which requires us to work very hard to realise and to sustain.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we succeed, it helps compensate for our lack of size.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By capturing the trade flows through the Straits of Malacca and Singapore, PSA became the largest container transshipment port in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a unique interchange in the world, connecting East and West, Europe, Middle East, India and China.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In addition to our seaport, we have also grown into an aviation node.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Before COVID-19 hit us, Changi Airport was one of the busiest airports in the world – and it shall be so again – though in aviation terms, our geographical location is not quite ideal.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We made it happen with a renowned Changi and SIA experience.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With these good global connections to the world, we built up the manufacturing sector, about one-fifth of our GDP today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We obviously do not manufacture just for Singapore, we are too small.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our exports also include trade in services and one growing services sector is financial services.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, almost every major global financial services institution is in Singapore, carrying out a range of activities including new ones such as fintech and green finance.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The financial services sector employs over 170,000 people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are also becoming a centre for technology, research and development.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many global technology firms – from FAANG to BAT and many more – are in Singapore and they make Singapore their regional or global innovation centres or engineering hubs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, around 50,000 international companies operate out of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Seven hundred and fifty of them have made Singapore their regional headquarters.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: None of this would have happened without a clear strategy, implemented well.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was a long and painstaking process, part of the story of our island-nation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Clean government, rule of law, safety, you can walk on the street any time of the day, political stability, good infrastructure, high standards of education, openness to the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All this and more come together and made us a good place to invest in and created many jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I should emphasise that another big plus point for us is the quality of the Singaporean workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our people are well known to be well educated, diligent, responsible, trustworthy and we get things done.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have one problem, which is that there are too few of us Singaporeans, a point which I will come back to later.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This brings me to the next topic: why FTAs, including CECA, are important to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We started our FTA strategy in the late 1990s.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We thought through it carefully and executed before other countries did.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It gave us a very precious early mover advantage and greatly boosted our efforts to export, attract investments and venture overseas, and created good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our total trade is three times our gross domestic product (GDP).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, when the Economic Development Board (EDB) goes out and persuades investors to come to Singapore, our network of FTAs is always a major selling point.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: FTAs are especially important to our small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They free them from being constrained by our small domestic market and give them access to global markets.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our SMEs are sending all kinds of Singapore-made products overseas: from canned food, barbecued pork, frozen roti prata – I heard some are exported to India – to medical devices, machines, components and chemicals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: FTAs are also spurring our companies to venture abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When our companies grow overseas, they become stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we accept this basic reality that Singapore needs the world to earn a living, then we would realise the fundamental importance of all our FTAs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are a keystone of the economic super-structure that we have built.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We could not have advanced the welfare of Singaporeans to the degree that we have without FTAs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Recently, we fell in the 2021 IMD World Competitiveness ranking from first place to fifth place.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Amongst the components evaluated, we continue to do very well in terms of Government efficiency and economic competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, we lost ground in terms of openness towards global talent and trade.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I hope this is temporary and due to the effects of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Overall, we are still holding our own in terms of foreign investments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the attacks on FTAs, especially CECA, have been very specific, let me now spend some time to explain how FTAs work.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And to prepare for this statement, I had to dig up my old negotiating notes and do quite a bit of revision and homework!

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The key disciplines of an FTA are as follows.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It requires a country to remove or lower tariffs on substantially all trade between the FTA partners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because other countries customarily impose tariffs on thousands of items.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We impose duties on only three alcoholic products: beer, stout and samsu.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In all my years of negotiating FTAs, I do not know what samsu is, neither have I drunk it before.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, any FTA that substantially removes tariffs imposed by both parties is inherently beneficial to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: FTAs also require governments to accord protection to foreign investments and ensure that regulations are imposed fairly and equally on both local and foreign firms.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They also set standards on protection of intellectual property.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Singapore, we always protect foreign investments and apply our regulations fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it has always been in our interest to do that.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Abiding to these principles and disciplines is not a problem for us at all.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, as more of our companies expand overseas and they create their own products, they too hope that Singapore can negotiate similar protection for them when they go overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The investment and intellectual property protection disciplines in FTAs are, therefore, important assurances for our companies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Newer FTAs also set certain environmental and labour standards.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Not every country supports them, but Singapore believes that they reflect contemporary concerns relating to free trade and investments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Specifically, on CECA, this FTA with India benefits Singapore in many ways.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Signed in 2005, it was India’s first comprehensive bilateral FTA with any country.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: CECA gave Singapore a strategic first-mover advantage in India, just when the continental country was taking off to be an economic powerhouse.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: CECA reduces tariff barriers, which made Singapore goods more competitive in the Indian market.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2019, 660 companies from Singapore have investments in India, almost double the number a decade ago.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As these companies grow regionally, they hire more people back home.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Despite these significant benefits, FTAs are controversial in many countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a trade negotiator, I have listened to the problems and sensitivities of many of our FTA partners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some countries wish to protect certain sectors, such as agriculture, that is a very common one, which Singapore does not do.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have some eggs, we have some fish but more for a bit of source diversification.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We never seek to conquer the world with our eggs and our seabass.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Others could not live up to, say, the transparency standards of government procurement or intellectual property disciplines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Still, others are concerned about the influences of foreign culture through industries, such as arts and entertainment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Canada, for example, is very sensitive about this area.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The toughest job and the most time-consuming job of a negotiator is to identify and understand the sensitive sectors, the sensitivities of your country and then find ways to protect or address them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We find words that give you comfort that address these sensitivities and we call these words in our jargon "exceptions" or "carve-outs".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When we have a big carve-out, with strong protection in our sensitive areas, we will say "this carve-out is strong and big enough for a jumbo jet to fly through!" In some sensitive areas, it is easy to negotiate "exceptions" or "carve-outs", because everyone agrees.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One example is right of taxation by governments; another one is national security; a third one is immigration.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Every country holds the view that there cannot be unfettered movement of people across borders.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That would create social unrest and a big public uproar.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Governments must retain the ability to impose immigration and border controls, and FTAs cannot undermine that.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, in all FTAs and also WTO Agreement, you will find that immigration powers are strongly and prominently preserved and protected.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You can find such standard clauses in the WTO Agreement, as well as in all our FTAs, including CECA.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As so many falsehoods have been said about the immigration-related parts of CECA, let me set out in some detail what is really in the agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Immigration matters are set out in Chapter 9 of CECA, "Movement of Natural Persons".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The legal text is available online, so I will only detail the salient points.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government retains full rights to decide who can enter the country to live, work, become PRs or become citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is clearly set out in two clauses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are standard clauses commonly found in all FTAs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And they are also the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 9 of CECA, so it is hard to miss them, as you can see them on the first page.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second point: the obligations relating to the Movement of Natural Persons in CECA, as in all FTAs, are not broad principles with wide applications, but actually highly specific.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What are these broad principles that you can find in FTAs?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One broad principle is that of National Treatment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is found in some chapters of the FTAs, such as Trade in Services or Investments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means, I mentioned this just now, you cannot discriminate against foreign service providers and investors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Whether they are local investors or foreign investors, you treat them the same.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Regulations and benefits that apply to local firms must apply evenly to foreign-owned ones.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, if immigration had not been carved out and the National Treatment principle had been incorporated into Chapter 9 of CECA, then indeed, Indian workers would have to be treated like Singaporeans, and would have had free rein to come to live and work in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Except that there is a strong immigration carve-out and National Treatment is not found in Chapter 9 of CECA, nor any other corresponding Chapter in the FTAs that Singapore has entered into.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, what then are the obligations of Chapter 9 of CECA?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are highly specific such as require "the Parties to process applications for temporary entry with some expedition, and with certain transparency", such as informing the applicants of the outcomes of their applications and not leaving them in suspense, a very reasonable thing to do and to agree to adhere to.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also have to accord a certain duration for the validity of the permits should we approve and approval must be based on them meeting our prevailing work pass conditions; also very reasonable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such a commitment on duration is also not something unique to CECA, because similar commitments exist in other FTAs and are also found in World Trade Organization (WTO) Agreement, signed by 164 Members, including Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many Parties to FTAs also commit not to impose labour market tests.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a common clause in our FTAs, including with India, Australia, China and the United States (US).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It means we do not insist that companies go through onerous processes and documentation to prove that no suitable locals will take a job, before they can hire a foreigner.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Companies in Singapore or any other places do not hire in this way.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What they do, the common and best practice, is to interview the suitable candidates, consider them all fairly and then make a judgement on the best person.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are all market-friendly, widely adopted, reasonable obligations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The listing shows the types of Indian professionals who may apply to work in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It does not mean that we must approve their application.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: India, for its own reasons, requested for such a list, similar to what they have in their FTAs with Korea and Japan.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, even if they had not listed the professions, their PMEs could still submit work pass applications to work here.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The list probably meant something to India because there may be countries that would not even let you apply.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is how protectionist some countries may become and India is trying to secure their interests there.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is, in fact, how other FTAs work: with or without listing of professions, nationals from our FTA partners are not precluded from submitting work pass applications, which will be evaluated based on our prevailing criteria and work pass conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Thus, the point being made by PSP on the list of the 127 professions is a red herring.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The list does not confer any free pass to any Indian national.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second common criticism is that intra-corporate transferees from India can also freely enter Singapore to work.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Based on my explanation on how the Chapter works, this is again not true.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Intra-corporate transferees also have to meet our work pass qualifying criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In any case, the total number of intra-corporate transferees from all over the world, and not just India, that have come to Singapore to work is very small.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, Mr Speaker, Sir, I hope we can put a stop to all this misinformation about our FTAs in general, and CECA, in particular.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Nevertheless, it is important that we recognise that PMEs in Singapore do face challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I see at least three challenges that they are facing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, there is more competition from foreign PMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Over this period, however, the increase in the number of local PMEs is much higher, by over 380,000.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, 380,000 for local PMEs and 112,000 for EP holders.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These numbers underline an important point: that competition between foreign and local PMEs is not a zero-sum game.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By combining and complementing local and foreign expertise, we can attract more investments and create many more good jobs and career choices for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The downside is that, with more foreign PMEs in Singapore, they can compete for jobs with locals at the company level and, at that level, there can be a zero-sum situation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, there is a trade-off at play here.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If I can put it simply: (a) many jobs, strong competition; (b) few jobs, no competition.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we need to find the right balance where there are more jobs, some competition.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is the way to advance the interest of Singaporeans; not swing to any extreme position, but strike that careful balance and then adjust if we find that that balance is off.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But if someone promises you many more jobs with no competition from foreigners, he is selling you snake oil.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It cannot be on any government’s policy menu.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I should point out that besides complementing our local workforce to create more opportunities, foreign PMEs also help cushion the impact on the local workforce when times are bad.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because during a downturn, foreigners bear the brunt of job losses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On the other hand, local employment has been stable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The unemployment rate for local PMEs in June 2020 was at 2.9%.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is from the labour market survey, so, it comes out only once a year during June and this is immediately after the circuit breaker.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Without the foreign buffer, when our economy ran into trouble, the situation would have been much worse.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, while the stock of EP and S Pass holders can fluctuate, Singaporeans enjoy greater security of employment, with help from various Government measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Jobs Support Scheme helped firms, helped enterprises keep their workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have a multi-Ministry National Jobs Council which came up with many initiatives to help place displaced Singaporeans into jobs, including the Jobs Growth Incentive, to encourage companies to hire local workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, when Mr Leong Mun Wai said in his Facebook post that we need to recoup a few tens of thousands of jobs from foreign work pass holders, he may not know that we have already done so.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second challenge is the profile of foreign PMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are concentrated in certain sectors and from certain countries of origin.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And when that concentration happens in areas, such as Changi Business Park, some may feel that we have lost a part of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Members of the House have raised this concern.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are taking this seriously and studying what we can do to lessen the problem.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I hasten to add that dealing with excessive concentration is not a straightforward matter of chopping up the operations of a company here.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We do not want to unintentionally cause the whole investment to move elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And this is part of the careful balancing that I talked about earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, at the company level, there may be unfair hiring practices, with department heads preferring to hire foreign PMEs, or even foreign PMEs from certain countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Whatever system we set up, there will always be some abuses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must tackle the abuses when they occur as swiftly as possible, while continuing to adopt sensible economic policies that are good for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOM takes a strong stance against such discriminatory practices and, together with our tripartite partners, has been actively enforcing against errant employers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Minister for Manpower will speak on this further.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have explained the underlying reasons for the difficulties faced by our PMEs, so that we know what it means for us in terms of public policy choices and how we can most effectively address the challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we mistakenly blame FTAs and CECA for these problems, our responses would be disastrously wrong and would make our problems worse.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government deeply understands the pressures faced by local PMEs in the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These include concerns about being displaced by foreign PMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some companies have employed more foreigners and this has made Singaporean employees uncomfortable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government has received feedback from many members of the public and Members of Parliament on these issues.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We take these concerns seriously and have already taken action to address them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In order to prescribe the right solution, we have to first identify the root cause of the problem.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, over the past year, before identifying the truth of the matter, the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) has laid the blame squarely on the India-Singapore Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA) as the main culprit for the unfettered inflow of Indian professionals, displacing Singaporeans from their jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: PSP also claimed that all the FTAs that we have signed have harmed Singapore's economy and the interests of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They have unfortunately turned FTAs into political scapegoats to discredit the policies of the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Their claims are incorrect and have distorted the facts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If anti-foreigner sentiments creep into Singaporeans’ psyche, the livelihoods of Singaporeans, the prosperity of the nation and the happiness of our next generation will be at risk.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Before joining politics, I was a civil servant and participated in negotiating FTAs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Therefore, I have the responsibility to correct all these baseless allegations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, what is the pillar of Singapore's economy?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are a small country lacking in natural resources.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The key to our economic success lies in whether we have a global view and whether we can leverage globalisation to attract foreign investments and expand into international markets to make up for our lack of natural resources and our small size.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Only by doing so can our people live in peace and happiness, and can young Singaporeans pursue their dreams.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, what is the intent of signing FTAs with various countries?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Through negotiations, we are able to get tariff exemptions from our partner countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This will help promote our exports and is especially important to our SMEs because the domestic market is too small.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These include ASEAN, China, the US, the European Union, Japan, Korea, India, Australia and New Zealand.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These are our major markets and also our important free trade partners.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: FTAs also help us to attract businesses and investors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: EDB often says that our FTA network is a major selling point to persuade MNCs when they decide whether to invest in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When investors come to Singapore, our FTAs can help them enter various major markets in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Also, under the FTA provisions, the Singapore Government has obligations to provide some protection to their investments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The listing of 127 professions serves as a point of reference for relevant parties.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fourth, where do the pressures that Singaporean PMEs face come from?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On one hand, we must remain open to create opportunities for our people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On the other hand, we must manage the competition it brings for our industries and people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, competition between foreign and local PMEs is not a zero-sum game.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A reduction in the number of foreign PMEs in Singapore does not necessarily translate into more jobs for our local people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, only by combining local and foreign expertise, can we attract more foreign investments and create more good job opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a small country that relies on the global economy, we face the following choices.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Option A, strong competition but many jobs; or option B, less competition but few jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What we need is to strike a balance.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To ensure that our people continue to have enough good jobs, some competition is unavoidable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If someone claims that he can give you an economic model that creates many jobs but no competition, he is definitely bragging and selling you snake oil.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another challenge that we face is that we are now growing our digital economy and our need for tech talent has grown.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, China and India are two of the largest global suppliers of tech talent.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many Chinese talent tend to work in China because they have many unicorn enterprises and significant domestic demand.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Therefore, there are relatively more Indian digital and tech talent in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a phenomenon that we have to face.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government is working together with industry players to explore adopting offshore outsourcing solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, this must be done carefully to avoid losing important foreign investments altogether.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must continue to discuss how to solve the problem, safeguard job opportunities and provide a level playing field for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Please do not listen to misinformation and reject FTAs and CECA.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These will erode the foundation of Singapore’s open economy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We note that many countries in the world are now facing the issue of xenophobia.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must not let this take root in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have to try our best to address the concerns of our people and resolve these problems for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, we need the cooperation of Singaporeans to defend the foundation of our prosperity together.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: (In English): I will switch back to English to conclude my speech.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As I explained earlier, our FTA strategy has benefited Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it is disappointing that FTAs are now a target of political attacks.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But, perhaps, I should not be surprised, as this has happened in many countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The question of global versus local has emerged as the new dominant political divide in democracies around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the US, labour unions and various industry lobbies are against free trade.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Trump Administration pulled out of the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) within a week of taking office, even though the US was the architect of the TPP agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the UK, Brexit was the culmination of a bitter political contest between those who wanted to be part of the European Union and those who wanted out.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In France, the next Presidential election is likely to be a face-off between the incumbent President Macron and the far-right nationalist candidate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: While globalisation presents opportunities and creates jobs, it also brings about greater competition, the displacement of industries and jobs, and inflow of immigrants.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These consequences go beyond the economic sphere and often strike at the heart of a nation and a community's sense of identity and security.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is the most unsettling change, causing people to become unsure if they are on the whole better off with globalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such concerns are genuine and deserve serious and proper attention.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are a small country and an unrestricted flow of workers from a large country can change the lived experience of Singaporeans, alter the character of our society and even overwhelm us.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we need to be careful that these valid concerns are not exploited by political groups and, intentionally or not, end up sowing division, stoking fear and fanning hatred.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As representatives of the people, we all have a responsibility to realise that our words and deeds can shape public opinion and the direction of our political discourse.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why when Mr Leong Mun Wai said in this House, some months ago, that the naturalised Singaporean CEO of DBS was not "homegrown" and deemed this a failure, Minister Iswaran responded with a word of caution.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I agree with Minister Iswaran and feel that Members of the House should be very careful about what we say on such matters, if we are not to give credence to very negative, even ugly, minority views.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is also why we appreciate the Leader of the Opposition standing up to say that when it comes to racism and xenophobia, we have to all reject them and there can be no "ifs and buts" about it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But even if Mr Leong Mun Wai and Ms Hazel Poa choose not to, I will be happy to clarify questions from Members.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a city state connected to the world, we want to welcome diverse talent from all over the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When they are here, we invite them to fit into our society, respect our social habits and norms, and appreciate our multi-cultural society, join us at the hawker centres, try durians, try some sambal belacan, speak a few phrases of Singlish.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I decided to make this Statement today, so that we can approach the debate on PSP's subsequent Motion with the right perspective and motivation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This House should continue to debate robustly the pros and cons of various policies to help Singapore navigate the balance between global and local.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The same goes for our openness to foreign workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We take the same approach when we decide on foreign workers coming to work in Singapore: how does it help Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are more than 2.3 million locals who are employed and our resident unemployment rate is 4.1%, half of what it was in 1970.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We need to understand the real challenges we are facing today in order to have a constructive debate on the way forward.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And that is why we are having these two Ministerial Statements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will explain with data, with details, as to exactly how our foreign workforce policies are implemented in order to benefit our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will also give our perspective on the real challenges we face today and the real solutions that are demanded.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Leong asked for the number of intra-corporate transferees or ICTs, professionals and dependants that come in through CECA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They all have to meet MOM's prevailing work pass criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Under the ICT route, the employer does not have to advertise on MyCareersFuture.sg, but the ICTs themselves are subject to additional checks on their seniority, on their employment history as well as their work and industry experience.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They are also subject to more conditions in their eligibility to bring in dependants and apply for permanent residency or future employment in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And if they have brought in dependants, the dependants do not have the automatic right to work here.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They can only do so if they qualify for a work pass on their own merits.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is a very fundamental point and I hope that everyone will remember this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Thus, and as mentioned by Minister Ong, the total number of ICTs has consistently been very small.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is 500 out of 177,000 Employment Pass (EP) holders in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As for the number of "professional visas" issued, I am afraid to disappoint Mr Leong, there is no such category within MOM.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Minister Ong explained, all 127 categories of professionals under CECA currently come in under our regular work pass framework.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The PSP has made Indian nationals coming in through CECA a focus of contention.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But I am afraid they have been barking up the wrong tree.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The number of ICTs coming in under our FTAs, and in particular CECA, is a very small number relative to our total number of EPs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I suggest we set aside this red herring and move on, more importantly, to the heart of the matter.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The heart of the matter is this: how do we, as a small country devoid of any natural resources, remain open to global talent for us to continue to create opportunities for our fellow Singaporeans while, at the same time, manage the attendant social repercussions?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They understand we need to remain open to global talent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In particular, they are worried about three things: first, that the growth in EP holders has come at the expense of our local PMEs; second, that some workplaces have become more concentrated with a single nationality; and third, that there may be discrimination against local jobseekers and employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I have come from the private sector, and I understand and empathise with these fears, these concerns and these anxieties.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am not suggesting that all of our approaches are perfect.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we will continue to refine them in the light of our experiences, always with a focused view to having a system that will and can deliver good jobs, good livelihoods and a thriving economy for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Not just for our generation but for our future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I hope this will enable us to arrive at a better understanding of the choices and the trade-offs that we constantly have to make.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, on the increased competition from foreign PMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In Singapore today, we have one of the best local talent pools in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But it is insufficient to meet the breadth, the depth, the needs of investments that generate the quality and the range of jobs that we have today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, when we bring in new investments, we will sometimes need to attract foreign expertise, foreign talent, while we build up our local capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Hazel Poa, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked for the breakdown of local and foreign workforce numbers by sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Given the issue at hand, let me focus on EPs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As of 2020, we have around 177,000 EPs, or Employment Pass holders, in our overall workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If you look at the top three subsectors: infocomm and professional services, these two sectors account for around one-fifth each; while finance accounts for another one-seventh.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This was also mentioned in Minister Ong's speech earlier on.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Over this period, the total number of local PMEs increased significantly by more than 380,000.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There have been questions asked, both inside and outside of this House, whether most of the growth in local PME jobs was accounted for by Singapore Citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If you look at our unemployment statistics, we provide the figure for Singapore Citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The citizen unemployment rate over the past 10 years has been consistently low, at around 3%.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Much attention has been placed on the finance and the infocomm sectors, which alone accounted for 40% of the increase in EP holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is significant but what is even more significant is that these two sectors saw even stronger job creation for local PMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We focus on these two sectors because they bring good quality jobs and Singapore, our beloved Singapore, can carve out an advantage and value-add significantly in these areas.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And as a result, there has been significant job creation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As we attract foreign banks, infocomm companies to create jobs here, they will inevitably need foreign workers to complement the Singaporean workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I want to deal with a fundamental misconception which lies at the heart of some of the things being misconstrued.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When a company decides to come into Singapore to invest and they need about 3,000 people, they may be able to find about 2,500 of these talents in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But they still need to supplement the 2,500 with the other additional 500 from overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If we object and we insisted that the balance of their 500 must all come from Singapore irrespective, then how do we expect that investment to take off?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: How do you expect an investment to come in?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These 2,500 jobs for the locals would be compromised greatly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The simple point is that while we have a good Singaporean talent pool, our pool is not large enough to fulfil all of the needs, the breadth and the depth of these enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Very often, foreigners also bring in skills which complement Singaporeans' skillsets as well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The misconception is that if we said no to the foreigners coming in, these jobs they would have taken would, therefore, all go to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: How do I know that this is a misconception?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They would love to take in Singaporeans if they could, because they would be more productive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But these jobs up till now are still not filled.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Perhaps Mr Leong would like to think deeply about that and deliberate and offer us some advice.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Leong also suggests that doing away with foreigners will reduce the displacement of our older PMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I wish that were so, but the private sector and the real economy do not operate this way.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There will always be displacement of PMEs, whether older or younger in any economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Industries change, companies downsize, they expand, they relocate, they pivot, they transform.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Regardless of whether you have foreigners or not, that would not change because this is the function of the business world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What matters most for us is whether we are able to find jobs for these displaced PMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To do this, we need an eco-system where there are also new companies willing to come and start up in Singapore, new investments, new foreign direct investments coming in and expanding multinational corporations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So far, I think we have done credibly in this regard.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: New jobs created have far exceeded the jobs that have been lost and our unemployment rate has been kept low.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And the re-entry rates for displaced PMEs are high.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That said, it is not always easy or possible to find every single displaced PME an equivalent job in the same industry, especially if there is a skills mismatch.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: An IT sales manager who loses his job may not find a job as a cybersecurity expert.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we do our best to help them find jobs in other growth sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If we tell companies which want to invest in Singapore that they can only employ Singaporeans, or first employ Singaporeans who have been displaced regardless of skills, I think the answer will be quite stark.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They, I think, will opt not to come into Singapore to invest.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: All companies will want to hire Singaporeans, but companies will also need to have that flexibility to hire the best available talent from around the world to complement our Singaporean workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I understand what displaced Singaporeans are going through.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Rest assured, we are doing our best to help you and your families.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But it is important that we go to the root cause of the problem, that we are able to tackle it and we are able to diagnose the situation accurately, and not provide treatment to just treat and relieve the symptoms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Because only when we can identify the right solution, we are able to prescribe, we are able to provide the precise and the appropriate treatment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The fundamental question now is, how do we strike a balance between ensuring that businesses have access to skillsets, to manpower, to grow and succeed, whilst creating opportunities for our local workers to grow and to progress?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our strategy to achieve this has always been two-pronged: ensuring that our workers can compete fairly and can compete strongly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, the first is to ensure that our local workers can compete fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We do this through our work pass controls.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our view, our prevalent view, is that foreign manpower should not come to Singapore just because they are cheaper to hire than locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They should complement but not displace our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They should bring in extra skills to help the companies and, at the same time, create more Singaporean jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In line with these objectives, at the Work Permit and the S Pass level, we have quotas.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And we have levies in place to regulate foreign worker numbers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have been progressively tightening quotas, we have been progressively raising levies to reduce manpower reliance, spur job redesign, push for quality growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Over the past decade, we have consistently and steadfastly held our course in spite of numerous calls from businesses to relax our rules.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We commit to productivity-led growth because we believe many of these jobs have the potential to be transformed into good jobs that provide higher real wages and rewarding careers for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For EPs, we do not impose quotas or levies because there is fierce competition for global talent and worldwide shortages in areas such as tech and digital skills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A quota would be a hard cap that would limit our ability to compete at the high end of the global economy, while for a levy to have any impact or any effect at all on EP numbers, it would have to be set very high and would substantially increase business costs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Instead, what we have done is that we have focused on setting and raising the quality bar for EP holders through requirements on salary and qualifications to make sure that the EPs who come in are at the right level and they bring the right skillsets, the necessary expertise and experience to contribute significantly to our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will continue to review and revise these thresholds regularly to ensure that they remain appropriate and they remain in tandem as our economy develops, as our skills, as our income levels, go up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Leong has also previously raised in this House his concern that foreign Employment Pass (EP) holders are cheaper to hire than locals, simply because their employers do not make CPF contributions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I think he fundamentally misunderstands the purpose of our CPF.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: CPF is set aside for our retirement needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As foreign PMEs who are not working in Singapore on a permanent basis, I do not think we should be responsible for their retirement adequacy or home ownership needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Hence, I do not think it makes sense for us to extend our CPF benefits and coverage to them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Fundamentally, our CPF system is designed to benefit our resident workers, not to help attract or deter foreigners.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Instead, when reviewing the qualifying salary to maintain a level playing field, we take into account CPF contributions as part of the cost to employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is packaged into the cost to employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Leong did not suggest that employers should pay foreigners CPF too.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Instead, he says he wants to impose a $1,200 levy on EP holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But as I have just explained, a levy is not the most effective or the right way to manage the population of foreign PMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I think that it would be better managed by appropriately setting the right salary level for entry into Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Hazel Poa has asked for numbers on dependants in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is relevant insofar as they are competing with locals for jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As shared previously, the vast majority of Dependant's Pass (DP) holders do not work during their stay in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In fact, Members would remember we have already regularised the work arrangements of DP holders in May this year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, they go through the normal work pass routes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There will always be calls from workers to tighten our foreign workforce policies further, just as there will always be calls from businesses to relax them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I can tell you that in my past life, I was also guilty of that.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I have also lobbied to relax work pass policies; that was a function of a listed company.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is the tightrope that MOM and MTI have to constantly navigate very delicately amidst highly competitive global markets for both investments and talent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ladies and gentlemen, there are limits as to how far we can tighten our controls without eventually hurting Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With remote working becoming more prevalent, companies increasingly do not need to site their manpower in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In fact, we may find more businesses simply choosing to move entire business functions offshore if it becomes too difficult, onerous or expensive to operate here.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singaporeans will end up with the shorter end of the stick as well by losing some jobs too.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is precisely why the second prong of our approach – that of ensuring that our Singaporeans can compete strongly – is just as important.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In an open and globalised labour market like ours, competition is intense and stiff.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There will be some of our fellow Singaporeans who are displaced from their jobs and we need to help them find replacement jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This happens not just because of competition from foreign workers but because of other factors like technological change and industries phasing out.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is why the Government invests so heavily in retraining and skills development so that displaced workers can gain new skills and reinvent themselves either by doing a different job in the same industry or transiting to another industry altogether.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In fact, for some industries, as they get sunsetted, we have to help workers to pivot and transform even faster.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is really the subject of the 23 Industry Transformation Maps that we have set up over the last couple of years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As Mr Lim Swee Say used to say, in Singapore, we are unable to guarantee your employment but rest assured, we will work very, very, very hard to ensure your employability.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Upgrading skills and staying relevant is, ultimately, our workers' best form of protection.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We do this through our system of education, through training and that goes beyond formal schooling.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We also help displaced Singaporeans through job facilitation and support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: COVID-19 has been an especially difficult time for many Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These programmes are in addition to long-standing programmes such as Workforce Singapore (WSG)'s career conversion programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To make our career matching services even more accessible to locals, WSG has set up in all 24 HDB towns SGUnited Jobs and Skills (SGUJS) Centres.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The retrenchment taskforce led by WSG and supported by NTUC's Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) reached out to nearly all retrenched local workers in 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar asked about the effectiveness of the different capability development schemes in building a local talent pipeline.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Within the first three months of implementation, the Jobs Growth Incentive supported 27,000 employers who hired 130,000 new locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With the support of employers and the unions, the policies that we have put up have preserved jobs for Singaporeans amidst the crisis of our generation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Total employment in 2020, excluding migrant domestic workers, shrank by 166,600.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Foreign employment took the most hit, shrinking by 181,500.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Resident employment, on the other hand, managed to expand by 14,900 in spite of the downturn.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are not quite out of the woods yet and there is more work yet to be done but, ladies and gentlemen, let us also build on what we have collectively achieved so far.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I want to talk about nationality concentration amongst foreign PMEs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Leong and Ms Poa have asked for the nationality profile of our work pass holders and their dependants from China, from India, from the US and from Australia.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Poa has asked for even more granular data on the sector and jobs commonly held by these same nationalities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am not aware of any country that reports at that level of granularity requested.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Nevertheless, we recognise that if misconceptions continue to spread, in spite of all of our attempts to address them in many other ways, even more damage will be done.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, I will share some numbers to address the misconceptions and allow for a meaningful engagement on the issue at hand.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The top nationalities that comprise around two-thirds of our EP holders have been consistent since 2005, namely, China, India, Japan, Malaysia, the Philippines and the UK.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I believe the interest is really in the Indian EP holders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In comparison, the proportion of EP holders from China has remained relatively stable across this same time period.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Is this the result of more favourable treatment for Indian EP holders due to the CECA?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As I have shared earlier, all work pass holders in Singapore have to meet the same criteria before they are allowed to enter our labour market.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Rather, these numbers reflect trends in the global demand and supply of tech talent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The larger increase in Indian EP holders compared to other nationalities is driven by the result of rapid growth and choices of growing our digital economy and finance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As every sector seeks to be digitally enabled, their need for tech talent has grown significantly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We do not have enough locals to fill the jobs available.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the infocomm sector alone today, 6,000 jobs currently remain unfilled.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Companies can decide which overseas countries they want to bring in their manpower from.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Based on their needs and the availability of the required talent, China and India, over the last decade or so, are two of the largest suppliers of tech talent.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But you would have read that China has sprouted so many unicorns and the Chinese companies themselves have a huge demand of their own.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, many Chinese talent decide to stay in China to work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I can tell you that these are the numbers that we are seeing across the construction industry amongst the migrant workers as well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I think prior to my coming onboard as the Minister for Manpower, many Members here would know that I deal with the dormitories most of the time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I can share with you the same statistics.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: India's talent, on the other hand, have continued to look outwards.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They also have the advantage of being English speaking.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: India has grown to become the second largest source of immigrants in the US and the third largest in the UK.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These two countries are also heavily invested in developing their technological capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our companies, our industries, our enterprises, they are both creators of technology and also adopters of the talent that is needed to create these technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Given our relative shortage of manpower, even if the workers do not come from India, they will come from somewhere else.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I hope that Mr Leong is not objecting to Indians per se.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The point I think we should ask ourselves is this: are they helping our companies?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Are they helping us to grow our economy and create better Singaporean jobs?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is not surprising, however, that this increasing concentration has caused some social frictions and anxiety to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In some ways, this is understandable and to some, we may even say that it is expected because these EP holders are transient.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They work in Singapore for a number of years and they contribute to our economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Apart from some EP holders who settle down and become PRs or Singapore Citizens, most of them, most EP holders work here for a few years and they either return home or they move on elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, it is to be expected that they are different and we do feel that they are different.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And this is the challenge of living in our multi-cultural society and a globalised world, as Minister Lawrence Wong spoke about recently.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is something that we will have to, and have been, proactively and constantly monitoring and managing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Indeed, when a single nationality becomes too prominent and that can have a disproportionate impact on our existing culture, our beliefs, it can cause our fellow Singaporeans, ourselves included, to feel less at home in our workplaces and in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the early 2000s, we experienced a similar situation when the share of PRCs in our foreign workforce increased significantly, before tapering as China’s growth took off.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Both then and now, the larger numbers did not go unnoticed and they created frictions within our communities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We understand these concerns, which is why we review and update our work pass policies regularly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We always seek to balance the needs of our economy with the needs of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have to bring in the talent and the skills to keep our economy growing, while tracking that the number of foreigners in our midst stays at a level that we are able to cope with, and manage the social frictions that will arise from time to time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is not going to be a once-off adjustment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will be a constant balance that we have to continuously monitor and get right.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, the Government does monitor the concentration of nationalities at the firm level.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In shortlisting firms, MOM looks at whether they have a high concentration of foreigners from a single nationality source, in addition to a high share of foreign PMETs relative to their industry peers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, being flagged in the FCF Watchlist is not evidence that the firm has committed any wrongdoing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Potentially, it could be a sign that some unfair hiring may be occurring.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The purpose of this Watchlist is to have the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices, or TAFEP, actively engage these companies to review and improve, where needed, their hiring practices and their human resource capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They respond positively and they exit the Watchlist.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For the small minority that are unresponsive, they can have their work pass privileges curtailed or they can be suspended for a specific time period.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are limitations in terms of the reach and the number of firms that we can put through this process.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will be looking to complement, to strengthen the FCF Watchlist with a more scalable approach.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As mentioned in MOM’s Committee of Supply (COS) speech this year, we are also exploring further refinements to our EP framework.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, we rely primarily on salary as a gatekeeper to select complementary talent, because this is easy to understand and administer.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
