text: But we are also exploring further additional refinements to achieve our objectives of a strong Singaporean Core, complemented by a diverse foreign workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I hope to share more details in due course.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Last but not least, I want to deal with discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: All employers are expected to comply with the requirements of the FCF and not discriminate on characteristics that are not related to the job.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When it comes to hiring foreign PMEs, employers must first advertise on MyCareersFuture.sg and consider all candidates in the local workforce fairly, before submitting a work pass application.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: TAFEP investigates potential cases of pre-selection based on proactive surveillance – we use data analytics and AI as well to find out.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, we actually sort of study the data quite aggressively.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We also receive complaints from the public and we act on them as well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Since its introduction in 2014, MOM has been progressively enhancing this framework.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa has asked about the results of our efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These cases are investigated by TAFEP and, where warranted, they are referred to MOM for enforcement.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Several Members of Parliament like Mr Louis Ng, Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Vikram Nair had earlier suggested strengthening our levers to give more bite to our Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We take these suggestions seriously and we have been studying various options.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ladies and gentlemen, on a fundamental level, the Government’s goal has always been to create a better life and a future for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We do that through growing the economy, through enlarging the pie so that more locals can enjoy better jobs and a higher standard of living.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We do that by tirelessly building up the Singaporean Core through a world-class education system, through continuous upskilling and reskilling; and we do that through working closely with all stakeholders involved to stamp out discriminatory employment practices and ensure a fair playing field to protect our Singaporean workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are careful balances and trade-offs to be made all the time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government is intent on keeping this balance right to achieve the goal of creating win-win outcomes for all.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM will always be both pro-worker and pro-business.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The power and the responsibility to make this happen does not lie with the Government alone.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They must win the confidence and the trust of their employees and the wider public by investing in a strong Singaporean Core, even as they complement it with a diverse foreign workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Workers, too, must adopt a growth mindset and continuously develop their skills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is the spirit of our Pioneers, who were resilient in the face of challenges and daring in new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Unions and trade associations and chambers, or TACs, must continue to serve as multipliers of these positive changes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They help to build the bridge between Government and businesses and workers and they have spearheaded important initiatives to help our businesses and workers transform and upskill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And I hope Members of all parties must take their responsibility as representatives of the people seriously and work towards constructive solutions and avoid exploiting divisive fault lines.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This tripartite partnership – between unions, employers and the Government – is the real reason why we have managed to succeed over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are at a critical inflexion point in our economic development.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The pandemic has caused significant economic damage the world over.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We face many challenges in the post-pandemic era, but there are also abundant opportunities if we play our cards right.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have distinguished ourselves internationally with how we managed COVID-19 and we have enhanced our trust premium.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Many businesses are now looking seriously at investing more in Singapore, which will create good jobs, but only if they can get enough workers, foreign workers as well, to supplement our local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If we can bring them in, we can continue to grow our economy for another five to 10 years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But if we lose this opportunity, we will not only take longer to recover, the impact will be borne by our older workers and also by our youths who will graduate into the workforce over the next few years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is a golden opportunity for Singapore to pull ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But if we turn protectionist and we make it difficult for companies to hire talent from around the world, then we will lose this opportunity.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A business hub means being cosmopolitan, having people from around the world, doing business with the whole world and creating more opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But if the competition is not here, it will be outside.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The competition would be helping other companies in other countries to beat ours here and displace our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Let us work together to continue improving Singaporeans’ lives and building a better future for all.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: (In Mandarin):   We have always put Singaporeans at the heart of our economic policies, and have always strived to create good job opportunities for Singaporeans and improve their livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singapore's open economy has contributed to our strong economic growth over the past few decades.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have not only attracted many multinational corporations (MNCs) to invest and set up regional headquarters here, but also helped many local enterprises seize opportunities to expand and venture into overseas markets.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Foreign companies, especially those in specialised or emerging sectors, will inevitably need to bring in foreign professionals to complement the local workforce with skills that are currently in short supply.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Nevertheless, such specialised capabilities can be transferred to local workers as these companies grow and develop.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Over time, local workers will acquire new skills which will in turn raise their competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I understand that the presence of such foreign professionals has caused some anxiety to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some Singaporeans may feel that they face stiffer competition for jobs compared to the past, or that they have been treated unfairly when applying for jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Others may worry about whether Singapore's social fabric will change.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The first is to ensure that our local workers can continue to have access to good job opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we have invested heavily in developing the skills of Singaporeans to ensure that they can maintain their competitive edge in the global market and succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As the saying goes, "Life is like the waves on the sea, with occasional ups and downs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Whether in good times or bad times, we still have to work hard." (In English): Somehow, it sounds different when I speak in Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is supposed to be sung in Hokkien.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I think even Mr Pritam Singh knows that it is a Hokkien song.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: (In Mandarin): Over the years, Singaporeans have gone through many ups and downs and never bowed to any challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: After all, we believe in "working hard to succeed".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the face of this crisis caused by the pandemic, Singaporeans have upheld the spirit of selflessness and adaptability of our forefathers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This shows that Singaporeans are willing to work hard, but we also care about being treated fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This requires the effort and cooperation of many parties.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, Singaporeans should continuously upgrade their skills and keep an open mind when looking for job opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government will provide comprehensive assistance to help Singaporeans tide over this difficult period and maintain a fair and just society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Over the past year, we have been hard at work dealing with the many challenges posed by the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At this juncture, I hope that we will stay united and uphold the Singapore Spirit.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government will work together with Singaporeans to overcome the difficulties ahead, emerge stronger from this crisis and build a better future for all.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I co-chair the NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce set up by NTUC last year to look into the concerns of PMEs and to flesh out a set of recommendations later this year in relation to employment and employability of PMEs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We have heard ground sentiments on a plethora of issues and challenges faced by Singaporean PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At the top of their mind is job security amidst this COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One concern, amongst others, which was surfaced is the intense competition from the influx of foreign manpower and anecdotes of unfair employment practices by employers who favour hiring foreigners and discriminate against our locals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Some PMEs shared with us their personal experiences of foreign hiring managers bringing in co-workers of the same nationality while others have shared about disguised discriminatory practices at work where they felt ostracised when their foreign colleagues, who form a majority of the team, communicate in their native language at work and through the unfair allocation of off-days given to their foreign colleagues during public holidays by their supervisors of the same nationality.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: While it is clear only a minority engages in such unacceptable practices, the concerns are legitimate and we should not ignore them.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: PMEs I spoke to acknowledge the need for FTAs and foreign manpower in this age of globalisation, global competition and economic survival and success, but we must recognise the need to support our local workforce's aspirations and to address their concerns and anxieties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One Singaporean PME who is an Asia Pacific Sales Director, as well as many other PMEs in those sectors with a higher proportion of foreign PMEs, such as the financial, ICT and professional services sectors, shared with me that we should not allow the import of non-specialised and non-highly skilled foreign manpower to compete against Singaporeans for well-paying jobs which many Singaporeans can do.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I think this principle of complementarity and not direct competition is an important concept which we need to continue to embrace and strengthen.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In other words, we will need to strike a balance between being open and having a level playing field for our locals with fair opportunities and fair treatment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This balance is not easy to achieve and is going to be an evolving process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Together with fellow Labour and PAP Members of Parliaments, I have been speaking and lobbying on this important area in and outside of this House the past decade to ensure fairness, equity and levelling the playing field, especially for our Singaporean PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We even set up the Employment Claims Tribunal, Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) as well as the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM), and issued many tripartite advisories, standards and guidelines to strengthen the Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am heartened that in these past 10 years of lobbying and advocating for a stronger Singaporean Core, many of these measures have been put in place, as shared by Minister Tan See Leng earlier, with the support of our tripartite partners and other economic agencies, such as MAS and EDB, to better support and protect our Singaporean workforce and provide them with a fair and level playing field in the job market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: That said, more needs to be done to strengthen the Singaporean Core, further develop our local workforce's capabilities and protect our locals from being unfairly discriminated.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is important to recognise the role that foreign manpower plays, which is to complement and enhance the capabilities of the local workforce and not to replace or displace it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In this vein, I would like to put forth some proposals to the Minister that aim to address fairness and localisation of PME jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I have previously submitted in this House on revealing or publishing the "triple weak" watchlist which MOM and TAFEP maintain, so that the potential reputational loss would serve as a deterrence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, we can level the playing field for local PMEs by enhancing the EP application review process to move beyond looking at the individual applicant's educational qualifications and salary, and pay close watch to sectors with a particular imbalance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will help to develop a pipeline of local talent.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To sum up, to say that we have found the silver bullet or antidote will not be an easy one as it is a treadmill journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need to constantly watch our step, keep pace and stay in touch with the pulse.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is important to state at the outset that the number of jobs in an economy is not an immutable datum.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, it is variable and it is the result of the net effect of the pace of job creation, which adds to the number of job vacancies and the pace of job destruction, which reduces the number of job vacancies.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the first few decades, after gaining Independence, the World Trading System under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) steadily reduced every race and lowered trade barriers.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The World Trade Organization (WTO) was established in 1995 as a multilateral institution that facilitated the signing of agreements in areas such as services, investment and Intellectual Property.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: This enabled the Singapore economy to attract MNCs to base production in Singapore, thus creating jobs and sell into the world market.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: With increased protectionist sentiments expressed in many advanced countries in recent years, the WTO has had difficulty in reaching new agreements.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It has been necessary for Singapore to turn to FTAs to provide a means to enlarge markets for Singapore-based firms.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: By negotiating and signing FTAs that enable our firms to export to destination markets with lower or zero tariff rates, Singapore can attract foreign capital to work in Singapore to employ Singapore-based workers and pull up their wages.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's rise in living standards over the past decades has been facilitated by a steady inflow of foreign direct investments, which brought technology and good jobs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, continuing to attract MNCs to base their production here, even as we become more service-oriented, with manufacturing hiring a smaller share of labour force, yet, doing this is likely to require a complementary set of skills that can be offered only by a combination of local and foreign workers, given the low fertility rate.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: At this stage of our development, where indigenous innovation must contribute to productivity growth, FTAs also allow new start-ups as well as both Large Local Enterprises (LLEs) and SMEs, to face lower trade barriers when selling into particular overseas markets.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, we continue to need to rely on MNCs because they are large, they pay better wages, but we are also at a stage where we need to stimulate indigenous innovation.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: But they need to have the capacity to be able to sell abroad.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, establishing FTAs that allow the partner signatories to the agreement to lower their tariff rates enlarge the market for our new start-ups as well as SMEs and LLEs.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, FTAs are helpful both from the point of view of continuing to attract MNCs to base their production here, but it is also important as a way of giving a lift to our more productive local firms, SMEs, to break into potentially neighbouring markets and further overseas.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The derived demand for workers resulting from the need to meet this external demand for our goods and services, like foreign firms and consumers in the partner countries who are signatories of the FTAs, will translate into the creation of new job slots, in particular, tasks.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A job is a combination of tasks that we create.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: So, the allocation of workers with the right skillset to fill these job slots with these particular set of tasks is necessary in order to maximise these Singapore-based firms' profit.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Only then will the productivity of the firm be boosted and the salaries correspondingly increased.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: If we succeed in doing that, then our resident workers will have the comparative advantage to fill these new job slots, the sort of thing that Mr Patrick Tay talked about.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Going back to Mr Ong Ye Kung's "Analogy A" of more jobs slots but more competition; and on the other hand, less competition and future jobs lost, he talked about being somewhere in between.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Given our history, the ability to ultimately compete in the world market says that there is something positive of a tilting towards the direction of increased competition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If I could ask Minister Tan See Leng whether moving forward, we will consider legislating the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I think that is important because it is not just discrimination based on nationality, but also based on race, religion, gender, family responsibility, disability, amongst many others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, I really hope we will consider legislating those guidelines.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An open debate based on the right information can only be beneficial to all parties involved, whether in or out of this House.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first one relates to Minister Ong's claim that PSP has made false allegations that CECA is allowing a free flow of Indian PMEs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I ask the Minister to provide the specifics of these false allegations that he mentioned, including details like when and where and who?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, will there be any more data forthcoming in the form of Written Answers?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, we agree that FTAs are important to Singapore's economy and we are not calling for the abolition of FTAs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our concern is over specific provisions in FTAs relating to the movement of natural persons.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In CECA, just now Minister Ong mentioned that the listing of the 127 professions does not mean that anybody who applies under this will be approved, but it can be rejected even if they apply.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourthly, under this clause, temporary entry and stay is up to one year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This agreement, you must understand, was negotiated by our current Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat and signed in 2005.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But then went on to state that the Government, I quote, "could not share the next level of details, including the number of Indian nationals converted to PR and those who subsequently gotten citizenships within the eight years under the intra-corporate transferee provision of the agreement." And then that starts to suggest that they come in and then become PRs and citizens as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Most recently, on 22 June 2021, in a Facebook post, Mr Leong Mun Wai said, "the most important economic policies that have affected the jobs and livelihoods of Singaporeans relate to foreign PMEs and Free Trade Agreements, in particular, the Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement with India." As Members of the House and also members of the public, through our handphones, we would also have received many other unattributable divisive messages coming through our feeds and chat messages.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think these quotes and all these messages you receive, if you are Singaporean, especially one facing challenges at the workplace, feeling insecure, you are bound to feel upset and angry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You are bound to feel, "I do not want to welcome foreign PMEs".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You will grow suspicious of them, even reject them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And that will be a natural reaction because the messages feed on our worries and our fears.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have seen how this has turned out in so many other countries, how the extreme right, nativist, populist parties have grown in strength, just by tapping into that fear and insecurity because of globalisation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But these far-right or nativist parties, they have been growing stronger in many places around the world and created divisions in societies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sometimes, they have replaced the governments who take a more moderate policy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I really hope that it does not happen here because if it happens in Singapore, as it happened elsewhere, our policies, our politics would have gone disastrously wrong.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Hazel Poa said that I promised to give all the data they requested.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But as Dr Tan See Leng explained, no country release data to that level of granularity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if I may just go back to my speech, what I said is, "Dr Tan will provide more detailed answers to the specific questions, including providing the data which will be useful for our subsequent debate and putting that data in context".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I did not promise that all the data will be tabulated and provided, and Dr Tan explained why.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We try to provide as much as we can, but I think there is a limit to what we can do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Hazel Poa also asked about Chapter 9 of CECA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As a trade negotiator, we always look out for the word "shall".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When you see "shall", it means you must do something.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you do not do it, you are in breach of the agreement.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You "shall grant temporary entry and stay up to one year for the duration of the contract." That is what we agreed to.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That means if we approve, if you meet our work pass conditions, we shall grant you one year of admission.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Imagine if you apply for something to the government, and then they tell you, "I approve but we do not know for how long"; tomorrow, revoke it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Remember, the ordering of the clauses matter as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I printed a copy and I highlighted the second and third paragraphs, the carve-outs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You read this Chapter, you know that this Chapter does not apply to immigration measures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then it goes on to say what the parties must then do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, later on in the Chapter, it says that you "shall" grant one year of approval should you approve.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I hope I have answered all of Ms Hazel Poa's questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I do have some questions too for PSP.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I tried to correct the falsehoods of CECA because the whole purpose of this Statement is that I know PSP is preparing for a Motion debate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I am also hoping that we all go into the debate with some common ground.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First of all, common ground must be, let us put aside the falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, I clarified which are the falsehoods and let us put them aside.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, CECA does not allow a free flow of intra-corporate transferees to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It does not oblige Singapore to approve the applications.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Approval is subject to them meeting our criteria.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the spirit of seeking common ground, we come to this House and we recognise that globalisation is a difficult thing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are lots of pros but there are also cons.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the case of Singapore, globalisation has allowed us to grow and to create a lot of good jobs and has benefited many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we had not done that, today, we will be having a very different kind of debate, of massive unemployment, of stagnating wages, of graduates not being able to find jobs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are two social downsides, other than the increased competition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, while foreign EP holders have come in to help us sustain our growth and though the growth in local PMEs outnumber that of foreign EP holders, the presence of foreign EP holders has nevertheless created more competition, discomfort and social issues.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, Singaporeans want to know that they will be given fair treatment at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have rules to achieve such fairness and we will continually review these rules and framework, and how they are implemented to ensure that fairness is assured.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is what the Government, on its part, has done in the spirit of trying to achieve some common ground as we go into the debate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, may I ask PSP, our two hon Non-Constituency Members of Parliament from PSP, after hearing all the explanations from Dr Tan and I, will you agree to the following?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a gross misunderstanding of the agreement and FTAs in general.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you agree to this, I think we have a good chance to have some common ground that when we come into the House again for a debate on the Motion, we can have a meaningful and constructive debate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If I may seek the clarifications of our two Members from PSP, please.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also thank Minister Ong Ye Kung and Minister Tan See Leng for their detailed explanation of the situation on foreign PMETs, foreign manpower, Free Trade Agreements and CECA.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As to Minister Ong Ye Kung's questions, I will leave them to the last or we will leave them to be answered in the debate that we are going to conduct later on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But there are a few things I would like to bring up here or a few questions I would like to ask to clarify the situation further.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We know the importance of FTAs for Singapore, as an open economy and especially as a small city state.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, what we are concerned about is what price we are paying.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first question I would like to ask is, in the process of negotiating an FTA, what are the bargaining positions that we can give?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I read things like, because we do not have many bargaining chips, the implication is that we may have to be a bit more relaxed with the movement of people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One question I want to ask is, is the movement of people or natural persons used as one of the bargaining chips when we are negotiating an FTA?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The whole purpose of PSP – as well as Hazel and I – bringing up the issue about foreign manpower or foreign PMETS or foreign talent, whatever term is used, and the FTAs is because it is about Singaporeans' jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When PSP's Dr Tan Cheng Bock raised the issue at the August 2019 launch of PSP, it is due to the huge amount of feedback that we got from the ground.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By raising the issue, we had hoped that we would get some response from the Government to explain more about FTAs, in particular, CECA.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: You may say that no one has come in through the CECA route but the clause is there.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is up to the other party, whether they want to use it or not and, most importantly, up to our Government to administer our employment policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because our employment policies are already quite relaxed in granting work passes to foreigners, so the Indian nationals do not have to come to Singapore through the CECA route.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the first question I want to ask is whether the movement of people is used as a bargaining chip.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second question I want to ask is, we should not focus on the number of people that got into the job market through the FTAs or CECA.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most importantly is how those conditions under the FTAs interplay with our domestic employment policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The next point I want to bring up or question is, the Government has admitted that something needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are concerns by Singaporeans regarding jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Have sufficient measures been taken to address them?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the questions I want to ask is, has the Government actually tried to find out what the total number of displaced Singaporeans is?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would think that you cannot deny that there are Singaporeans who are displaced.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Your narrative is that it is because they do not have the skills.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us not push the blame to the Universities and the Polytechnics so easily.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has been 20 years since we started the foreign talent policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They would like to have the job that was taken by a foreigner, but were not able to.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They lost their current job and when they got another job, they got a lower pay.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is also a significant number of Singaporeans who are under-employed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If you look at the growth of the Grab driver population, the growth of our traineeship programme and many of our independent workers, are they voluntarily opting for the independent lifestyle or are they facing difficulty in getting a permanent job?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fourth question is, of course, we are particularly concerned about the finance and the IT sectors.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister Tan See Leng has given some numbers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unfortunately, we do not have enough time to digest those numbers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think the Minister might have given some figures just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fifth question is, the Minister said that we are not competitive, Singaporeans are not competitive but —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, I would urge you to stick to the facts.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think we have all been participating in this debate and listening intently, so I do suggest that you keep to what has been said.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: A lot of questions have been answered as well.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The idea of a debate is to debate the issues that have been raised, so please do that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, we are happy to take the time to debate whatever that is meaningful, but please make it meaningful.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not understand what you mean by meaningful, because I am going through those points.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The fifth question is, we have had this foreign talent policy for 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But if you look at the way MOM has administered and regulated the flow of foreign PMETs into Singapore, you find that the policies, of course, over time, there is a bit of tightening at a time but, generally, it seems to be too little and too late.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: At the kind of threshold salary plus no CPF, do you think we are attracting the right foreign talent into Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My sixth question is, I totally agree with Minister Tan See Leng about what we are driving at, it is not abolishing things, it is not totally eradicating things.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are also talking about a rebalancing, but the rebalancing cannot come as a result of a natural attrition from COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There must be a policy recognition that whether our past foreign talent policy was on the right track or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If we review the policy and we think that there are certain things that we need to change, then make it a policy point.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Do not allow natural attrition to come by and say tens of thousands have left Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is not the way we conduct policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I respect you for your experience in the private sector, Minister Tan.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As an employer, is that not a wage concession?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, how can we say that Singaporeans are not being treated unfairly in the job market competition?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Again, I will raise the point which I have said just now: then what happened to our education system?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What happened that after 20 years, you are still telling Singaporeans that we have not enough talent?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, we are not saying that we can substitute the foreign PMETs completely.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But at least there can be some rebalancing, and we get back to my question just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And if the Minister admits that there is some displacement of Singaporeans, then that rebalancing means we must slowly allow Singaporeans to be given the first opportunity to take up the jobs first.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My last question is, the Minister talked about diversity, but here again, is it not something that MOM should have done long ago about diversity in the workforce when we introduced our foreign talent policy?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We also know, because we have worked in an international environment before, that the group dynamics at the workplace can change very fast with changes in the nationality composition in the company.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, especially when MOM is monitoring and regulating the granting of the work passes, do you mean you have not, at the beginning, taken that as an important consideration?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And, today, then you have to say that, "On my watchlist, I have this number of companies that have a very large concentration of PMETs from a single nationality".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we really want to understand how MOM actually administers this whole foreign PMET policy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: After this, maybe I will add a few more points, I will ask a few more questions about the approval process, some of the experiences I had in the private sector with regard to MOM and its approval process.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But my questions are these questions for now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a long list of questions which I am not sure would help us bring the discussion forward.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Four to eight is for MOM but I think let us not prolong this because, as Mr Speaker has noticed, many of the questions were actually addressed in our speeches.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if you do not accept what we say, there is very little room for us to further explain.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I gave examples of our port, airport, financial services, ICT, manufacturing, you name it, we are a hub of all hubs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Investors come here, they want to hire Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They know our education system is solid and we have such a wonderful reputation around the world, something that, as Singaporeans, we should be proud of.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The education system is a bit stressful still, but we should be very proud of that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The problem is, there is still not enough of us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are some questions, and we have given figures, so I do not think I would answer those.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He mentioned a whole series of procedural policy, how come the Fair Consideration Framework came in so late, why is the salary bar for entry raised only later.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOM's successive Manpower Ministers have been reviewing policies all the while.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Old policies worked for a period of time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, when China and India grew, you get a different influx of workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You need to adjust your position, hence, you review.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And this process will continue and we will debate in this House on the pros and cons of prevailing and new policies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You cannot say because we implemented something new now to respond to the situation, therefore, we have failed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why did you not do it five years ago?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If it were so, then, for every Bill that is tabled in this House, we have failed, because we should have tabled this Bill five years ago.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will go back to the first three questions that the Member posed to me, but actually I posed to him first.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Hazel Poa made a point, if I heard correctly, she said, "We are not against FTAs, we support the FTAs".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I thought we started to have some common ground.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: She is not a trade negotiator, so, I think those are fair questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have been a trade negotiator for many years, I explained how the chapter ought to be read.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And when she asked that, I hope it is because she might have read the chapter wrongly to think that Singapore shall allow professionals from 127 categories to enter, no questions asked.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: After my explanation, I was hoping that she would come to the conclusion that they might have interpreted the chapter wrongly but after hearing Mr Leong Mun Wai speak, I think my assumptions are all wrong.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I had two questions for the Members and was hoping to hear "yes" to both.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do not think you are taking it back.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Please prove me wrong, but after hearing you, I am afraid these are your positions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I guess it is because of the fact that, for quite a number of the issues, I think he is looking at it, first and foremost, from a hindsight kind of perspective: why is it that we did not do this, why is it that we did not do that?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We started with a very conscious effort in the 1970s to go and build heavy industries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: There were all these heavy industries that we built up.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our Pioneer founding generation leaders under former Minister Mentor Mr Lee Kuan Yew, Dr Goh Keng Swee and so on, I think at that time when we first started, we were very, very heavily invested in these heavy industries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We did disk drives, wafer fabrication and then, eventually, in early part of 2000, we went into services, we went into bio-pharmaceutical, life sciences and so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And now, we are into tech, we are into infocomm and we are into finance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Every 10 to 15 years, we have seen fairly dramatic transformation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think it is inconceivable that you would expect that policies that you enact do not get refined, do not get tweaked and do not get adjusted over time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I guess to his point about the fact that why is it that we did not do this and so on, I think in the last 15, 20 years – and he has sort of pointed out the fact that I have been from the private sector; perhaps, I have not been in the Government long enough – if anything at all, for the last 20 years, change was the constant.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Change is a constant and change will be a constant.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continually face disruption, we will face transformation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, to his other point about why is it that we are not able to have all this workforce ready in spite of all of our education upgrades and so on, I think if we all had a crystal ball 20, 30 years ago and we could gaze so clearly into the future, perhaps, even for himself, as a CEO of a private equity firm, I think all the necessary investments made would have been perfect and spot on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But, perhaps, I think, hindsight, like what they always say, is perfect.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the other point about private sector and how we package the CPF into it, indeed, I can share with you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Perhaps my experience is very limited; I have just been in healthcare all my life.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do admit that I lobbied at that time, five, six years ago, for an increase in the number of S Passes because of the fact that I needed to deliver a certain level of nursing care.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I just could not hire enough healthcare personnel, for example, nurses, to come in and help us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: While we do not pay CPF, the overall costs of bringing them in is higher because we have to package in housing and other allowances.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And, really, because the employer part of it is imputed into our cost, I can tell you with conviction, because I have done it for many, many years in my life, that that package that we pay out is higher than what we do pay to locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The only difference of course is the overtime charges and so on.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I think that is another sort of thing altogether.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the Member's point about the education system, I just want to share one bit.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The entry levels, in terms of the grades, the credits and so on, that are required for the students to make it to get into the Universities are also significantly higher.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I guess the point of this is that every single initiative, every single policy, we can always do better.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And that is something that I have acknowledged.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But the point is this, we are not that far worse off.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our glass is not even half full; our glass is three-quarters full.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we are looking at it from that perspective.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Are you saying that we should even adjust that?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Of course, we should try to bring it up to 90% or 100% full.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But let us also be mindful of the sentiment, the worries and also the hard work of the other three-quarters in that glass that is three-quarters full.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I look forward to a robust debate with Mr Leong and Ms Poa.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think when they can put up questions which I do not struggle so hard to follow, that would be very welcoming.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think, Mr Speaker, you will agree with me that we really need to move on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And to move on, can I go back to my two questions for the two hon Members from PSP?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If they agree, I think we can have a meaningful debate when they table the Motion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As I said, the answers to the two questions actually require a bit more debate and study.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But, first, I want to say that PSP and Hazel and I, we are for FTAs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Having heard that jobs and livelihoods of our people are not being used as a bargaining chip, we are very reassured that our interests, Singaporeans' interests are being taken care of.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, whether CECA has contributed to the overall influx of nationals from that country, I think we need to study a bit more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because we have to go back and look at the numbers provided by the two Ministers to see what is the share of the Indian PMETs in our overall PMET workforce and to take into consideration what Minister Tan See Leng has said about how we really need them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, at least, that is common ground that we have established.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If I hear him right, I think he is confirming that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He is not sure about the overall balance of the Free Trade Agreement.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think we will leave it there for our debate later on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I think these two, I will say, form quite good common ground, but it will also mean —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, I will call you when it is time to call you.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And it will also mean, naturally, that PSP will take back their allegations that CECA has led to an unfettered flow of Indian professionals into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I have said is that we fully support FTAs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We know that that is important for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And we appreciate the point that we are not using the movement of people as a bargaining chip in the negotiation of the FTAs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I think at least we got you to say FTAs and CECA are fundamental to our survival.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if you continue to allege, notwithstanding all our explanations, I think there is no choice, we have to leave it as such.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is regrettable because generations of FTA negotiators worked very hard to make sure our interests are all protected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is not an avenue for any professionals from any country to enter Singapore with a free hand and unfettered.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I take it that this is PSP's position, notwithstanding and after hearing all our explanation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is most regrettable but we will have to accept how they feel.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: On behalf of the business community, I thank both Ministers for their Ministerial Statements.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Contrary to closing the doors, the businesses are begging, "Please open the doors, we need workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Otherwise, who's going to do the work?" Nonetheless, if I may, I am a product of Singapore’s MNC strategy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And during the Budget Debate and COS, I have shared my views in regard to embracing diversity of talents from all over the world, so that we can be uniquely competitive.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, for today, I will not go there.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I will talk more about FTAs, in support of FTAs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A lot has been said but, perhaps, if Members can bear with me for a while, I will talk, from the business community, why is this important.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As a small and open economy without natural resources, we are highly dependent on international trade and highly integrated, well-functioning global value chains.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: International trade not only provides us with the products that we import and consume, but also connects us to the global market that supports our businesses and sustains our economy, creating the good jobs that Singaporeans have enjoyed in the past and aspire to for the future.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With Singapore’s international trade more than three times its gross domestic product, our livelihoods and prosperity depend heavily on international trade.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For Singapore businesses, free and open trade, premised on the foundation of a rules-based multilateral trading system, is crucial to ensuring a conducive, stable and predictable environment.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly important for us, considering that we are just a little red dot.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, the FTAs yield tangible value to our companies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These FTAs accord our businesses preferential market access into the markets of our major trading partners, lowering entry barriers for the export of goods and services, as well as protecting their investments in other countries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This strong FTA network can be a tool for businesses, not only in reducing their costs and time-to-market, but also in ensuring a predictable trading environment.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I would dare say that because our Singapore businesses remain very much plugged into our FTA network, we have been able to ride the storm of COVID-19 a little better than if we were disconnected.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We should know first-hand what it Is like to be disconnected, considering the impact we experience in aviation and tourism because of border closures.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Trade, along with foreign direct investments into Singapore, will drive our economic recovery and the resumption of business activities post-COVID-19, even as we restlessly reinvent our industries, innovate ideas, products, services and business models to emerge stronger post-pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Through this crisis, businesses have realised the urgent need to build resilience in their business models and supply chains, partly by exploring new markets and supply sources.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Many have shifted away from lean supply chain models to adopt agile supply chain strategies and the FTAs are even more relevant than ever before for our businesses.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has dramatically accelerated digital transformation to the top of the board’s agenda in every company.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As we have heard the Minister for Trade and Industry yesterday, MTI and the Government agencies have been hard at work looking into various new opportunities for us to enter into new trade agreements, including for renewable energy, green economy and so on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: On that count, frankly speaking, on behalf of our business community, I would like to acknowledge the efforts of MTI, MOF and all the Government agencies in helping our businesses to be competitive.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In order to help our companies familiarise themselves with Singapore’s FTAs and improve their global competitiveness, the business community, supported by SBF, holds regular workshops as well as seminars and provides complimentary advisory services to assist the Singapore companies on FTA-related enquiries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses can utilise these available resources and leverage SBF to provide feedback on how existing and future FTAs can better serve their needs, and we will continually do so.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We will need to navigate the pressing issues that adversely impact supply chains and business processes.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Across industries, developing the DNA to tap into overseas markets and to trade with multilateral partners is critical for businesses to be successful, given Singapore’s limited domestic market.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: FTAs offer a key tool for businesses to expand into new markets, enhancing accessibility of different markets by allowing businesses to export more freely and easing some of the regulations.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: But Singapore and Singaporeans must humbly recognise that we are vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We need to exercise humility and restlessly reinvent ourselves.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, I believe, as Singaporeans, we should be concerned as well.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, let me give you a very brief history of FTAs because I was in MTI at that time, first, as a Deputy Secretary and then as a Permanent Secretary.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: In 2000, the Doha round of WTO negotiation was launched and then-Minister George Yeo and I were at Doha.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: We saw the entry of China into the WTO.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: But soon after the launch, our assessment and Minister George Yeo's assessment then, was that it looked like the Doha round would not go very far.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: And he said, what does Singapore need to do to ensure our continued survival?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung earlier mentioned the importance of free trade to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, he decided that we should pursue Free Trade Agreements, and our very first Free Trade Agreement was with New Zealand, two small little economies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: And I must say that people were laughing; what could two small little economies do to advance the cause of free trade?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: But we persisted and we got the first agreement done and, thereafter, we went on to do a number of other agreements.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: When I was Permanent Secretary, I was in the trenches negotiating many agreements with our ASEAN counterparts.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: And that is how we had the ASEAN Economic Free Trade Agreement; that was enhanced to the ASEAN Economic Community.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: One was Free Trade Agreements between Singapore and other countries, far bigger economies: Japan, Australia, US; and then, more recently, the European Union.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: And what is that as a bargaining chip?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: But I think a very important quality for our public policy is that we must be creative and we must learn to meet the needs of other countries to see what may be in the agreement that is of benefit to them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, how did we manage to negotiate trade agreements with big economies that have a lot of concerns?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: For example, Japan was very concerned about agriculture.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: In the case of India, there was an even wider range of concerns.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, let me tell Mr Leong and his team that I spent three years of my life negotiating this agreement because although I was a Permanent Secretary – and Permanent Secretaries usually just supervise, they do not get into the trenches – the Indian side decided that it was an important agreement, they would have a permanent secretary, and Minister George Yeo said, "Well, you have no choice".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, I ended up being the chief negotiator for CECA.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: I can tell you the amount of homework I had to do to look at how we can come to an agreement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: I went to different parts of India because there was objection from every part of India, from business groups to states.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: Because this is of great importance to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: You have a population that is over a billion.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: Singapore has a population of, at that time, probably about three-odd million, and I said we will be easily swamped.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, we must have very strict agreements on this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: And that was, in fact, among the last chapters.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: There were two chapters that were the most difficult to conclude for which I never let go and we got what we needed.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, I think Mr Leong Mun Wai must not think that, well, you said, "I hope that the Government has the people's interests at heart".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: Why do we negotiate FTAs and why do we do this in public service if it is not with the interest of our people at heart?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: Why do I spend three years of my life doing the agreement?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, please be reasonable and do not mislead Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: I want to raise two other issues which are very important too.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: First, you said, "Why is it that we do not have talents and what happened to our Universities?" Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean was the Education Minister.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, was I, and all our former and current Education Ministers are sitting here.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: I must say that I am extremely proud of what our schools and our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) have done over the years to groom Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: The World Bank has ranked Singapore the best in the world in educating our people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: We have Polytechnics and ITEs which provide the most valuable practice-oriented learning.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: We have now the Earn and Learn Programme and a whole range of programmes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, I think, Mr Leong, you will better serve Singaporeans if you help Singaporeans understand how changes are taking place so quickly and you must help to encourage people to upgrade and learn new skills, and work to support our unions in forming Company Training Committees and Job Security Councils and the like, in order to raise the ability of Singaporeans to compete.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, I think to say that our education system has not done a good job or that the Government has not put in enough, I would seriously ask you to rethink that, and come back and debate us on that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: Prof Hoon Hian Teck made an excellent point that the future of competition will be a future of competition of innovation and technology.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: And it is very important for us to bring in some of the best people to work with Singaporeans, grow Singaporeans to be able to excel in that new realm.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: It is going to be a different world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, please do not get stuck in the old world and think that we can excel all on our own.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: Let us have an open attitude to work with countries around the world who are willing to cooperate and work with us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: France is not a small country and they have a long history of science and innovation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: So, that is a very important point that Prof Hoon Hian Teck had made.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: The other important point is from Ms Janet Ang, who talked about digital opportunities and the new market.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: No sector in our economy is going to be immune from competition.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: Economists used to have this concept of tradable and non-tradable sectors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: Non-tradable sectors are naturally protected because they are in your neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat (East Coast)
text: Your neighbourhood shops, who is going to compete with them?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I just have two supplementary questions: one for Minister Ong and one for Minister Tan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For Minister Ong, in 2016, my parliamentary colleague and Workers' Party Member of Parliament Leon Perera asked the then-Minister for Manpower – and this was arising out of feedback from the ground about CECA – issues about a lot of Indian nationals working on the ground.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And the question Mr Leon Perera asked was about the number of intra corporate transferees (ICTs) that were working in Singapore through CECA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At that point, the reply that came was the Ministry does not disclose the data on foreign manpower with breakdown by nationality, including data on ICTs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In February this year, Mr Leong Mun Wai of PSP asked a question about the number of ICTs working in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The point I want to make to the Minister and to the Government at large is the opportunity to quell or at least to nip some of these issues in the bud when they start moving into the realm of xenophobia and nativism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One important way to prevent that is the availability of information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In August 2020, a Straits Times reporter mentioned that "ICTs were a key bone of contention with respect to CECA".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If this information on the number of ICTs had been made known earlier, it does occur to me that a lot of the misunderstanding and the reaction we see about CECA could have been addressed and actually nipped in the bud.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government understands that with more information, actually, we can hold the line better before these discussions move into a realm of xenophobia and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My question to Minister Tan See Leng pertains to TAFEP and the strengthening of the enforcement arm of TAFEP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We had an exchange at the opening of Parliament about this and I would just like to confirm with Dr Tan whether raising the numbers in the enforcement arm of TAFEP is on the cards and what discussions have taken place since August last year insofar as how TAFEP will be beefed up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party has a position about anti-discrimination legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is that something that MOM will be prepared to look into?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The suggestion that he talked about, the position he had alluded to, in terms of legislation and all that, it is not something that has just come out from the Workers' Party.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you go back in terms of the past proceedings, I believe that quite a number of the Labour Members of Parliament, including Mr Patrick Tay and even non-Labour Members of Parliament, such as Mr Louis Ng, have also raised it at different times.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As I have alluded to in my speech, Mr Pritam Singh, I think you will appreciate the fact that given where we are today, it is a very tight rope that we are navigating.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the one hand, we want to continue to strengthen, to tighten.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the other hand, businesses have the competing interest of asking us to be a bit more lax.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are fully cognisant of the angst, the fears, the worries about making sure that there is fair, there is equal opportunity in terms of capability development, capability transfer, fair hiring, promotions and so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not want to sort of go down a prescribed route today because we are exploring the entire universe.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung, if we can wrap up the debate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will answer the question from the Leader of the Opposition and then seek to conclude this debate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I take to heart what the Leader of the Opposition has said, that with information, we can quell such falsehoods much earlier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some data is classified secret, confidential and so on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we are not at liberty to always disclose them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some information, it is better for it to come out early and then we can move on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Especially, as you said, when it concerns issues like racism or xenophobia, it is much better to quell it early.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you disagree and I misrepresented you, please jump up and correct me.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Deputy Prime Minister and myself are former trade negotiators, fighting in the trenches with our fellow teammates, which is why I think we both felt compelled to say something today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Negotiating an FTA requires a lot of dedication and hard work.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It takes a toll on the family because you are out of the country all the time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our negotiators are up against very formidable partners sometimes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our job is to advance Singapore's interests while protecting our areas of sensitivities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we work hard at it, nevertheless, because we know it makes a huge difference to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When we explained how an FTA works and how Chapter 9 works, it is a statement of fact.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not a matter of your opinion or your perspective.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, we can discuss employment policies, how we can better protect, educate, train our workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But PSP did not do the logical thing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I could not hear a definitive position from Mr Leong Mun Wai or Ms Hazel Poa.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They waffled a bit and then I think what I heard was they cannot conclude either way now whether CECA is better or worse for our workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if you cannot conclude either way, then the honourable thing is to also withdraw the allegations while you figure out which way you want to lean.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I do not think what we saw was logical or honourable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A successful FTA strategy is not just about negotiating skills.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Those are important but, fundamentally, it requires us to be broad-minded and able to cast our sights far and wide to the whole world and work with like-minded partners out there.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is why COVID-19 is such an existential crisis for us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It has forced us to close our borders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I am confident that once we get the great majority of our population vaccinated and control the pandemic, we can re-open the borders progressively again.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What I am worried about is, even when our borders are re-opened, what about our hearts and our minds?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If, because of COVID-19 or during the COVID-19 pandemic, anti-foreigner sentiments and xenophobia creep into our collective psyche, then even if our borders are open, our hearts and minds are not and will remain closed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I say we should emerge from COVID-19 announcing to the world that Singapore continues to be that shining jewel in Southeast Asia: the largest transshipment port in the world; the special Changi experience; the financial services hub and IT capital; a hub for manufacturing, hospitality, meetings, incentives, conventions and exhibitions (MICE), and so on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You can experience the richness of many cultures and also the uniquely Singapore character.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Singaporeans will benefit immensely from this because of the opportunities it brings and of how the international linkages and relationships cement our position in the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every one of us know that because we all did our part – whether it is getting vaccinated, undergoing regular testing, observing safe management measures, helping others in need, taking care of patients – all of us did our part.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Unity is what helped us conquer and overcome this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Speaker
